title: Test data: normal, boundary, invalid, erroneous
specPoints: 2.3.2 Select and use suitable **test data**: **normal**, **boundary**, **invalid** and **erroneous** data
Design a **test plan** with expected outcomes and compare with actual outcomes
learn: Define the four types of test data and choose examples for a given program
Explain why boundary data finds the most logic errors
Write a test plan table: test number, purpose, type, data, expected result, actual result, pass/fail
Run a test plan against a real program and act on failures
Answer 'suggest suitable test data and justify it' questions for full marks
hook: A program accepts marks from 0 to 100. I will give you three numbers to test it with and you tell me which ones are a waste of time: 50, 51, 52. All three are the same test. What would you choose instead? (0, 100, −1, 101, 50, 'fifty'.) Those six are a test plan.

video.title: Four kinds of test data
video.brief: 4 minutes. A number line 0–100 for a mark. Normal data lands in the middle (green). Boundary data lands exactly on 0 and 100, and just outside at −1 and 101 (amber, 'where bugs live'). Invalid data lands far outside (red, 150). Erroneous data is the wrong type entirely — the word 'fifty' falls off the number line. Then a test plan table filling row by row: data, type, expected, actual, pass/fail. End with the one failing row and the fix.

explain.code:
Type        What it is                                     Mark 0–100 example     Expected behaviour
Normal      Typical, valid data the program should accept  45, 72                 Accepted, processed correctly
Boundary    Data at the very edge of the allowed range,    0, 100 (just inside)   Accepted
            and just outside it                            -1, 101 (just outside) Rejected with a message
Invalid     Right type, but outside the allowed range      150, -40               Rejected with a message
Erroneous   Wrong type / cannot be processed at all        "fifty", 3.5, blank    Rejected without crashing
after: OCR's wording: **normal**, **boundary**, **invalid**, **erroneous**. Some textbooks merge invalid and erroneous; the exam accepts 'invalid' for both out-of-range and wrong-type if explained, but using all four and labelling them correctly is the safe answer.

p: Most logic errors are comparison mistakes — `>` for `>=`, `range(1, 10)` for 1–10 — and those only show at the edges. A program that passes with 45 and fails with 100 has a boundary bug. Always test the exact limit values **and** one step beyond them.

explain.code:
No. | Purpose                     | Type      | Data   | Expected result        | Actual | Pass?
----+-----------------------------+-----------+--------+------------------------+--------+------
1   | Typical mark accepted       | Normal    | 45     | "Fail" output          |        |
2   | Lowest allowed              | Boundary  | 0      | "Fail" output          |        |
3   | Highest allowed             | Boundary  | 100    | "Pass" output          |        |
4   | Pass mark exactly           | Boundary  | 40     | "Pass" output          |        |
5   | Just below pass             | Boundary  | 39     | "Fail" output          |        |
6   | Just above range            | Boundary  | 101    | Error message, re-ask  |        |
7   | Far out of range            | Invalid   | 500    | Error message, re-ask  |        |
8   | Wrong type                  | Erroneous | "ten"  | Error message, no crash|        |
after: **Expected result is written before you run.** That is the whole discipline: if you decide what should happen after seeing what did happen, you are not testing. Every rule in the program (pass mark 40, range 0–100) gets its own boundary tests.

p: 'Give an example of boundary data for this program and explain why it is suitable' — give the value **and** say which limit it tests: '100, because it is the highest mark the program should accept'. 'Complete the test plan' — fill the expected column from the program's rules, not from guesses.

list: **Boundary**: right on the edge (0, 100) and just over (−1, 101).

p: Most bugs are `>` when it should be `>=`. Those only show up at the edge numbers. Always test the exact limit and one past it.

simple.h: A test plan is a table
p: Columns: number, what it tests, type, data, what *should* happen, what *did* happen, pass or fail. Fill in 'what should happen' **before** you run.

keyterms.def: Inputs chosen to check whether a program works correctly.
Typical valid input the program should accept and process.
Values at the edge of the valid range, and just outside it.
Data of the right type but outside the acceptable range.
Data of the wrong type that cannot be processed, e.g. text where a number is expected.
A table of tests with data, type, expected result and actual result.

try.title: 1. Choose the data
p: A program asks for a person's age (0–120) and tells them whether they can vote (18+). Write a test plan of at least 8 rows covering all four types and **both** rules (range and voting age), with expected results.

try.title: 2. Run your plan
p: Run the program against every row of your Try 1 plan. Fill in Actual and Pass/Fail. At least two rows will fail — find the bugs and fix them, then re-run the plan.

try.title: 3. Make it survive erroneous data
p: Use `try`/`except ValueError` (or `.isdigit()`) so that "eighteen" and a blank entry produce a message instead of a crash. Then add rows 9 and 10 to your plan for them.

try.title: 4. Test someone else's function
p: Here is a function that is supposed to return the grade for a mark: 90+ A, 80+ B, 70+ C, 60+ D, else U. Write a test plan with every boundary, run it with a loop, and list which marks give the wrong grade.

try.title: 5. Classroom assessment: test-plan builder
instructions: Build a test plan for one of your own programs in the tool and export it.

check.q: For a percentage input (0–100), which is boundary data?
Typing "abc" into a field expecting a number is:

opts: Comparison errors (> vs >=) only show at the edges
It is the only type the exam asks about

check.q: In a test plan, the expected result is written:
opts: Before running, from the program's rules

check.q: For a pass mark of 40, the best pair of boundary tests is:
check.fb: Either side of the rule's edge.

exam.q: A program accepts a quantity of tickets from 1 to 10. Give **one** example each of normal, boundary and erroneous test data for this input, and state the expected outcome for each.
model: Normal: e.g. 5 (1), accepted and processed (1). Boundary: 1 or 10 (or 0 / 11 just outside) (1), accepted (or rejected with a message if outside) (1). Erroneous: e.g. "five" or 2.5 (1), rejected with an error message without crashing (1).
exam.commentary: Six marks: value + expected outcome × 3. The expected outcome must match the value chosen — '11, accepted' loses the mark. Invalid (e.g. 50) is also fine where the question allows it.

exam.q: Explain why a programmer should test a program with **boundary** data as well as normal data.
model: Boundary values are where comparison and loop-limit errors (e.g. using > instead of >=) occur (1), so a program can work for normal data and still fail at the limits; testing boundaries finds those errors (1).
exam.commentary: Mechanism (comparison errors) and consequence (works for normal, fails at edge).

exam.q: Complete the test plan for a program that outputs "Child" for ages under 13, "Teen" for 13–19 and "Adult" for 20 and over. Four rows are given: 12, 13, 19, 20. State the type of each and the expected output.
model: 12 — boundary, Child (1). 13 — boundary, Teen (1). 19 — boundary, Teen (1). 20 — boundary, Adult (1).
exam.commentary: All four are boundaries (each side of the two rule edges). Expected outputs come from the stated rules, not from running anything.

home: Write a full test plan (at least 10 rows, all four types) for your 2.2 capstone quiz program, run it, record actual results, and fix any failures. Hand in the plan with pass/fail completed.

teacher.timing: 60 min: hook 4 · explain 10 · try 30 · check 5 · exam 8 · homework 3
misconceptions: Boundary means 'any large number'. It means the exact edge and one past it.
Filling the expected column after running. Collect plans before Try 2 if needed.
Testing only one rule when the program has several (range *and* pass mark).
'Invalid' and 'erroneous' swapped. Right type/wrong value vs wrong type.
say: 'Where exactly does the rule change? Test one each side of that line.'
'Expected first. Then Run. Never the other way round.'
teacher.skip: Try 5 optional. Try 1 → 2 → 3 is the full cycle and should not be cut.
differentiation: Support: Try 1 with the data column filled; students supply type and expected result.
Stretch: Try 4 — write the tests as `assert grade(90) == "A"` lines and explain what an assertion is.
